title: Count Special Subsequences
statement:
`nums` is an array of positive integers. Count the index quadruples `(p, q, r, s)` with `p < q < r < s` that satisfy both rules:

- `nums[p] * nums[r] == nums[q] * nums[s]`;
- no two consecutive chosen indices are neighbours: `q - p > 1`, `r - q > 1` and `s - r > 1`.

Return how many such quadruples exist.
notes:
## Intuition

Checking all quadruples is O(n⁴). Rewrite the rule as a ratio instead: `nums[p] * nums[r] == nums[q] * nums[s]` holds exactly when `nums[p] / nums[q] == nums[s] / nums[r]`. Each quadruple then splits into a left pair `(p, q)` and a right pair `(r, s)` that only have to agree on one fraction. For a fixed `r`, the left pairs allowed are those with `q <= r - 2`, and the right pairs those with `s >= r + 2`. A hash map counting the fractions of the allowed left pairs answers each right pair with a single lookup.

To compare fractions exactly, reduce each one by the greatest common divisor and pack it into one number, `top * 1001 + bottom` (both parts are at most 1000).

## Approach

1. `ratios` maps a reduced fraction to the number of left pairs that have it; `count` is the answer.
2. Move `r` from 4 up to `n - 3`. The only newly allowed left pairs are those with `q = r - 2`, so add the fraction `nums[p] / nums[q]` for every `p <= q - 2`.
3. For every `s >= r + 2`, add the number of left pairs whose fraction equals `nums[s] / nums[r]`.
4. Return `count`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 3, 6, 1]` has seven elements, so `r` can only be 4. Then `q = 2` and `p = 0`, giving the fraction `1/3`. The only right pair has `s = 6`, and `nums[6] / nums[4] = 1/3` matches it once, so the answer is `1`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n² log M), where M = 1000 bounds the values: each of the O(n²) pairs is reduced once with a GCD.
- Space: O(min(n², M²)) for the distinct fractions in the map.

## Pitfalls

- Pair `p` with `q` and `s` with `r`: the fractions are `nums[p] / nums[q]` and `nums[s] / nums[r]`, not `nums[r] / nums[s]`.
- Add a left pair only once its `q` is at most `r - 2`; adding it earlier breaks the gap rule.
- When every value is equal the answer is close to 4 · 10^10, so Java and C need a 64-bit total.
- Rounded-down integer division merges different fractions; reduce with a GCD instead.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `ratios` | reduced fraction → number of allowed left pairs with it |
| `count` | special quadruples found so far |
| `p`, `q`, `r`, `s` | the four indices |
| `ratioKey`, `divisor` | packs a reduced fraction into one number; the GCD it divides by |
| `key` | the packed fraction of a left pair |
